implementation_notes: The standard library now ships both halves: std::barrier is reusable and calls its completion function once per phase - in exactly one thread, before any party is released - which is the leader/aggregation slot of the pattern; std::latch is the single-use downward counter whose count_down() plus wait() pair is the fan-in gate, with arrive_and_wait() as the combined worker-side call. Reach for the hand-rolled form only below C++20, and note that std::latch has no reset at all, so a loop must use std::barrier or construct a new latch per round.
pitfalls: std::latch is single-use: reusing it in a loop is impossible (no reset exists), and std::barrier::arrive_and_drop() changes the party count for every later generation - document which one the loop uses.

The completion function runs inside the barrier, before other parties are released: blocking there stalls the phase, while throwing violates the nothrow completion requirement and can terminate the program; keep the callback small and report failures through shared state.

A participating thread that exits or is cancelled leaves the barrier permanently short of its party count; C++20 barriers have no timeout or broken state, so exception safety must rethrow after arrive_and_drop() or propagate through a side channel.

variants.name: Pre-C++20 hand-rolled barrier and latch (mutex + condition variable)
variants.idiom_name: std::mutex + std::condition_variable with a generation counter
variants.implementation_notes: Below C++20 the structure is written by hand: a mutex, a condition variable, a remaining-parties counter and a generation number. Each arrival locks, decrements the counter, and either releases everyone of the current generation (bump the generation, notify all) or waits until the generation changes behind a predicate. The same class covers both usages - reusable while the counter is reset each generation, one-shot when it is not - and the classic form remains justified only where the toolchain cannot use C++20 or where a non-standard notification policy is required.
pitfalls: A bare cv.wait() without the generation predicate wakes on spurious wakeups or on the next generation's release and lets a straggler run ahead of its phase.

The release must happen after the state change; notifying while still holding the mutex is legal but hands the awakened thread a lock collision, and forgetting the notify converts the barrier into a permanent hang.

An exception in one participant breaks the generation: without an explicit abort flag plus broadcast the remaining parties wait forever, so the failure policy is part of the hand-rolled class, not of its callers.
